question.knowledge_point: Finding Points Where a Tangent Vector is Parallel to Another Vector
question.problem: Given the curve $r(t)=⟨\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}+4t,3{t}^{2}+9t⟩,$ find the point at which the tangent to the curve is parallel to the vector $⟨1,3⟩.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we calculate the derivative of $r(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}+4t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{t}^{2}+9t)⟩ \\  & =⟨3t+4,6t+9⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The vectors ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $⟨0\,,\,1\,,\,3⟩$ are parallel for some specific value ${t}_{0}$ of the parameter $t$ if and only if there exists a constant $c$ such that ${r}^{′}({t}_{0})=c⟨1,3⟩.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =c⟨1,3⟩ \\ ⟨3t+4,6t+9⟩ & =c⟨1,3⟩ \\ ⟨3t+4,6t+9⟩ & =⟨c,3c⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the components gives:

$$
{\begin{aligned}3t+4=c \\ 6t+9=3c\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we obtain that $c=3t+4.$ Substituting $c=3t+4$ into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}6t+9 & =3(3t+4) \\ 6t+9 & =9t+12 \\ 3t & =-3 \\ t & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $⟨1,3⟩$ and ${r}^{′}$ are parallel only at the point corresponding to $t=-1.$

Finally, since

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-1) & =⟨\frac{3}{2}(-1)^{2}+4(-1),3(-1)^{2}+9(-1)⟩=⟨-\frac{5}{2},-6⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

we conclude that $⟨1,3⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(-\frac{5}{2},-6).$

evidence.solution_quote: we conclude that $⟨1,3⟩$ and ${r}^{′}(t)$ are parallel at the point $(-\frac{5}{2},-6).$
